title: Ash-Sharh: with hardship, ease
hook: with hardship comes ease, said twice (94:5–6)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ash-Sharh, the opened chest. Your line was the burden lifts. When your chest got tight, did you stop for three wide breaths? Day one hundred eighty-five.

Some sentences get written on hospital whiteboards, taped above desks during exam season, tattooed on wrists, texted at three in the morning to a friend whose marriage just ended. In the Muslim world, one short Qur'anic line might be the most shared of all. You'll see it in Arabic calligraphy on living-room walls, on phone lock screens, on the last page of a student's notebook. It's said twice in a row, and the way it's worded is more hopeful than most people realize. Today: Ash-Sharh again, with hardship, ease.
screen: `ON WHITEBOARDS, WRISTS, LOCK SCREENS.` → `SAID TWICE IN A ROW.` → `MORE HOPEFUL THAN IT SOUNDS.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: the opened chest, the lifted burden, the raised name. Then the surah says, in Pickthall's translation: But lo! with hardship goeth ease, Lo! with hardship goeth ease. Notice the first small word: ma'a, with. Not after hardship. With it. The ease isn't only waiting at the end of the hard thing; it's already inside it, traveling alongside. Scholars point out that even the worst stretch usually has something in it that holds you up: a friend who shows up, a night of good sleep, a moment of laughter at the hospital. Now notice the grammar, which classical scholars loved. In Arabic, hardship is al-'usr, with the word the: the hardship, the same one both times. But ease is yusr, without the: an ease, and then another ease. So the same hardship, said twice, meets two different eases. A saying reported from early Muslims puts it this way: one hardship will never overcome two eases. Scholars discuss how firmly that saying traces back, but the reading of the grammar is widely taught. Then the surah ends with what to do: when you're free of one task, keep working, and turn to your Lord with longing. Not sit and wait for ease. Keep going, toward Him. The surah was revealed to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ in hard years, when the followers were few and the pressure was heavy. It didn't promise that the hardship would vanish. It promised company for it. With hardship, ease.
screen: `MA'A — WITH, NOT AFTER.` · `THE HARDSHIP, AND AN EASE.` · `ONE HARDSHIP, TWO EASES.` · `WHEN FREE, KEEP WORKING, TOWARD HIM.` · then, large: `WITH HARDSHIP, EASE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name the ease inside a hard thing. Sit, and bring one hard thing to mind, something you're in the middle of right now. Don't try to fix it. Just look at it honestly. Then look for what's traveling alongside it. A person who's helped. Something you've learned. A small good that came only because of this. Name one ease. Then look again, and see if there's a second. The bell holds the time.
Ash-Sharh. The opened chest, and the surah that says twice: with hardship comes ease. Today's word.
Your line: with hardship, ease. Send the line to one person going through something hard today. Or keep it for yourself, and look for the ease that's already there. Day one hundred eighty-five.

howItsDone: Muslims often quote 94:5–6, inna ma'a al-'usri yusra, to comfort each other in illness, loss and hard times, and the verse is common in calligraphy in homes and on cards.

fork.setup: you've just finished a hard task, and ease has come. what does the end of the surah say to do?
options: keep working, and turn to your Lord with longing
fork.reveal: when you're free, keep striving, and turn to your Lord (94:7–8). the ease isn't a stopping point.

original.note: Arabic: an ease, indefinite; set against al-'usr, the hardship, in 94:5–6.

trapdoor: what you thought: after bad times come good times.
what it means: ease comes with hardship, alongside it, and the verse is repeated for emphasis.

what a scholar hears: definite al-'usr repeated is one hardship, indefinite yusr repeated is two eases; the saying 'one hardship won't overcome two eases' is attributed to Umar and Ibn Abbas, with chains scholars discuss.
